query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying controlled thermomechanical treatment—specifically, systematic rolling and annealing experiments with well‐defined temperature and strain rate parameters—will improve phase stability, refine the microstructure, and optimize material properties.
generation.material_initial_state: An alloy in an initial cast or as-processed state with potentially suboptimal phase distribution and relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the material to a thermomechanical processing route that combines precise rolling (deformation) and annealing (thermal exposure) treatments.
generation.conditions: Processing over a range of temperatures spanning from non‐equilibrium to near‐equilibrium, with controlled strain rates to allow simultaneous monitoring of phase changes, grain refinement, and property variations.
generation.structural_mediator: The induced grain refinement and phase transformation resulting from the interplay of thermal energy and mechanical deformation.
generation.mechanism: Controlled thermal activation combined with deformation increases dislocation density and promotes phase transformation, leading to refined grain structures and stabilized desirable phases. This enhanced microstructure is expected to translate into improved mechanical (and potentially other functional) properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The material will exhibit increased phase stability, a finer and more uniform microstructure, and optimized mechanical properties such as enhanced strength and ductility compared to states produced by standard heat treatment or deformation-only processes.
generation.baseline: Materials processed by conventional methods that use either heat treatment or deformation independently, resulting in less tailored microstructure and property profiles.
generation.boundary: The improvements might be limited if the processing conditions do not adequately span the non-equilibrium to near-equilibrium range or if specific alloy chemistries respond differently to the applied thermomechanical parameters.
generation.uncertainty: While the general mechanism is well-supported in materials science, the precise magnitude of improvement in any given alloy system remains uncertain and will require empirical tuning of the processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several identical alloy samples and subject them to controlled thermomechanical treatments with varying temperature and strain rate profiles. Include control samples processed by isolated heat treatment or deformation. Characterize the phase stability, microstructure, and mechanical properties post-treatment.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification and stability
Scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructure and grain size analysis
Mechanical testing (tensile/compression tests) for property evaluation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed by combined thermal and deformation treatments do not show statistically significant improvements in phase stability, microstructure refinement, and mechanical properties compared to the control groups, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
